newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yaohan Japan hard-hit by persistent debt worries.
newsitem.headline: Yaohan Japan hard-hit by persistent debt worries.

text.p: Persistent speculation that Yaohan Japan Corp is having problems paying its creditors caused its shares to tumble for a fifth consecutive day on Thursday and forced the Japanese retailer to hastily call a news conference to deny the rumours.

Yaohan Japan, the flagship firm of the Yaohan international retailing group, on Thursday denied a media report that it may seek court protection from creditors under the weight of hefty loans as a result of the group's aggressive expansion overseas.
"I've never dreamed of seeking court mediation from creditors, or been prepared for it," company president Mitsumasa Wada told a late evening news conference in Tokyo.

Earlier, the mass circulation daily Yomiuri Shimbun reported in its wire service that Yaohan Japan was in talks with financial firms on possible changes in the retailer's restructuring plan and that it may be forced to apply for court mediation.
Wada said he is not considering holding talks with banks, but added that Yaohan has asked some of its suppliers to accept a delay in payments worth some 5.5 billion yen ($48.6 million).
The Yaohan group has aggressively expanded its business overseas, especially in China, resulting in hefty interest-bearing debt.
Yaohan Japan runs a chain of supermarkets in Japan.

Under restructuring plans unveiled in February, Yaohan would halve interest-bearing group debt to 90 billion yen ($796 million) over the next two years through the sale of stores and offices as well as part of its overseas assets.
The media report came only a day after rumours circulated in the stock market that Yaohan may fail to honour promissory notes. These rumours were later denied by the company.
The market speculation sent Yaohan's shares tumbling to a record low of 133 yen on Wednesday.

Shares in Yaohan have shed about 70 percent so far this year, ending the Thursday session at 143 yen, a record closing low. Yaohan was the biggest percentage loser on the first section of the Tokyo Stock exchange (TSE) on Thursday.

Market participants and analysts said that there was a widespread view that the Yaohan may run into difficulties in gaining much-needed support from its creditor banks to restructure its business, which could worsen its financial situation.

"It's natural to think that way," said Akishige Ishikura, an analyst at Dai-ichi Securities Co Ltd. "That kind of speculation could persist for a while... But it would even be positive for stocks if firms in bad shape were to disappear."
Private credit research firm Teikoku Databank Ltd said Yaohan is burdened with 170 billion yen ($1.50 billion) in debt.
"Yaohan is apparently in a hand-to-mouth situation," said one industry watcher, who declined to be named.

Tokai Bank Ltd, Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd, and Sumitomo Trust & Banking Co are among the major creditors of Yaohan, but none of them would say whether or not they were now in talks to give financial support to Yaohan.

An official at Teikoku Databank's information section told Reuters that some more firms rumoured to be in a fragile financial state could follow in the footsteps of general contractor Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd in going bust.

Tokai's failure last Friday showed that banks, which are still saddled with massive problem loans from the "bubble" era of inflated asset prices, are hesitant to take risks by extending loans to firms in trouble.

"Banks have cast votes to decide whether to let a company go under," the Teikoku official said. "With the financial strength of banks becoming weaker, more firms could go under after failing to win what (support) they used to get from banks."
